To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the oligochaete N. pardalis builds a tube by secreting a substance that sticks sand grains together and that it selects small sand grains for ingestion.

Nais pardalis lives in the surface layer of sandy sediment in Loch Leven by secreting a material which binds the grains together, and that this animal selects the smaller grains in its environment for ingestion.
Nais pardalis forms its tubes by secreting a mucus that sticks grains of sand together.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a small freshwater oligonchate, Nais pardalis, which lives in the surface layers of sand sediments in Loch Loven, Kinross, Scotland.
the behaviour of Nais pardalis, a small, common, freshwater oligochaete from Loch Leven, Kinross, Scotland, in the laboratory and in its natural habitat.
the local distribution and behaviour of the oligochaete N. pardalis Piguet.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the behaviour of N. pardalis is not random, that it is not directed towards any particular objective and that it is not adaptive.

Nais pardalis lives in Loch Leven in the surface few centimetres of sandy sediments, that it constructs tubes by the secretion of an adhesive, that it ingests sand grains and that it does not construct its tubes by the active ingestion of grains and their subsequent extrusion.
the behaviour of this animal is such as to ensure that the tubes are kept clear of sand grains, but that it has no control over the size or shape of the tubes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the behaviour of this animal is such that it is able to live in the surface few cms of a sandy sediment, but it is not clear why it should be so.

the animals are able to select sand grains from a population of grains which is heterogeneous with respect to size and that they are able to do this in a manner which allows the animal to eat grains at a rate which is not limited by the size of the gut.
the behaviour of the animal is not directed at the construction of tubes in the sediments, but that the tubes are formed incidentally to its behaviour.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Nais pardalis, a small freshwater organism, lives in the top few centimeters of sandy sediments, and it does not actively build its tubes, but instead secretes material that binds the sediment grains together.
Nais is a very efficient sediment engineer.
N. pardalis has an unusual feeding behaviour that is likely to be widespread among other oligochaetes.
